Seeing Your Daily Money Clearly

Before you can manage money, you need to see it moving. This module maps how money enters and leaves your hands each week, compares the real cost of cash, bank apps, mobile money and POS agents, and ends with an honest check of where you are starting from, including how safe your accounts are.

Two women can earn about the same each month and live very differently. One gets to month end with something left and can handle a surprise cost. The other borrows from a neighbour every third week. Very often the difference is not income. It is **how daily money decisions are made**, especially in the days just after money arrives.

This course is about the everyday side of money: the cash in your purse, the balance in your bank or mobile money app, the transfers you send and receive, the bills that keep coming back, and the requests from family and friends. You will use your phone as a simple tool, not a complicated one. Budgeting theory, savings groups and loans are covered in other WODDI courses; here we focus on what happens between Monday morning and Sunday night.
Money in, money waiting, money out

Every household has the same three parts. **Money in** is everything you receive: salary, sales from trading, payment for a service, money from a spouse, a child abroad or a cooperative payout. **Money waiting** is where it sits before you use it: your purse, a box at home, a bank account, or a wallet app such as OPay, PalmPay or Moniepoint. **Money out** is everything you spend or give: food, transport, data, school costs, rent, contributions and gifts.

The plan step sits between waiting and spending; most money trouble starts when that step is skipped.

The step most people skip is the plan. When money arrives, it is spent in the order requests appear, not in the order of importance. The loudest need wins: the child who asks first, the seller who calls, the snack at the bus stop. A plan simply decides, before spending starts, what each part of the money is for.
Timing: the problem behind many shortages

Income rarely arrives at the same rhythm as costs. A salaried worker may be paid on the 25th, but food is bought every day and the electricity token runs out on a random Thursday. A trader earns a little every day, but the shop rent is due once a year. This mismatch creates **gap days**: days when the money for a need has already been spent on something else.
Monthly income, daily spending: the risk is spending too freely in week one, then struggling in week four.
Daily or weekly income, large occasional costs: the risk is that rent, school fees or a gas refill arrive when nothing has been put aside.
Irregular income (a hairdresser, a caterer, a tailor): the risk is treating a good week as normal and a bad week as an emergency.
Worked example: finding the gap days in a salary month
For example, Ngozi is a school administrator in Enugu paid about ₦120,000 at the end of each month (an illustrative figure). She keeps no plan and spends as needs appear.
Week 1 she spends ₦48,000: foodstuff ₦25,000, a family contribution ₦10,000, data and airtime ₦5,000, transport ₦8,000.
Week 2 she spends ₦36,000, including a new pair of shoes for ₦12,000 that was not planned.
Week 3 she spends ₦28,000. Her balance is now ₦120,000 minus ₦112,000, which is ₦8,000.
Week 4 still needs about ₦8,000 for transport and ₦10,000 for food, so she is about ₦10,000 short and borrows.
With a plan she divides the month into four weekly amounts of ₦30,000 and releases one amount each week.
The shortage was not caused by low pay but by front-loading: ₦84,000 (70%) left in the first two weeks. Weekly releases of ₦30,000 remove the week-four gap if she stays within each week's amount.
Giving each naira a job

A daily-money plan does not need to be long. On one page of a notebook, or in your phone's notes app, write your expected money in for the coming week. Below it, list the jobs that money must do in order of importance: food, transport to work or market, bills due this week, money for the business, something set aside, and only then wants. If the jobs add up to more than the money, you cut or delay before spending starts, not after you run out.
Write the money you expect in this week, and the day it arrives.
List fixed jobs first: food, transport, bills due, business stock.
Add an amount to set aside, even ₦500.
Add wants last, with a clear limit.
If the total is too high, reduce wants first, then look for cheaper ways to meet needs.
Weekly beats monthly for most people

Even if you are paid monthly, plan in weeks. Seven days is short enough to remember and long enough to see a pattern. Move one week's money into your spending wallet at a time and leave the rest where it is less tempting.

Finding the charge before you pay it

Charges change over time and differ by provider, so this course does not give fixed amounts. What you can always do is **look before you confirm**. Bank and wallet apps show a fee line on the confirmation screen before you enter your PIN. POS agents set their own charge for cash withdrawals, and it usually rises with the amount. Ask the agent the charge out loud before the card is inserted or the transfer is made.
In your app, start the transfer and stop at the confirmation screen.
Read the 'fee' or 'charges' line. If none is shown, check your statement after the first transfer.

Worked example: what small charges cost in a month

For example, Halima runs a provisions kiosk in Kaduna. Customers pay her by transfer, and she withdraws cash from a POS agent almost every day to buy stock and pay her assistant. The charges below are illustrative; use your own agent's real figures.
She withdraws ₦10,000 five days a week. Her agent charges about ₦200 each time.
Weekly charges: 5 × ₦200 = ₦1,000.
Monthly (about 4 weeks): 4 × ₦1,000 = ₦4,000.
She changes her routine: she pays her main supplier directly by transfer and withdraws ₦25,000 twice a week instead. The agent charges about ₦400 each time.
New weekly charges: 2 × ₦400 = ₦800. Monthly: about ₦3,200, and her supplier now has a transfer record.
Halima saves about ₦800 a month in charges and, more importantly, makes fewer cash trips and has a record of supplier payments. Small changes in habit, not a new app, made the difference.
Fake credit alerts

A text message that says money has arrived is not proof. Fake alert SMS messages are a known trick. Before you hand over goods or cash, open your own bank or wallet app and check that the balance has actually increased.
Keeping digital money safe
Use only providers licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria. Deposits in licensed banks are also covered by the NDIC deposit insurance scheme up to a set limit.
Your PIN, password and the one-time password (OTP) sent by SMS are yours alone. No genuine bank staff member, agent or customer care line will ask for them.
Turn on the app's own lock (fingerprint or code) and your phone's screen lock.
Keep the bank's official customer care number saved from its website or the back of your card, not from a WhatsApp message.

If a transfer fails but you were debited, keep the screenshot and transaction reference and complain through the bank's official channel. If it is not resolved, the CBN has a consumer complaints process.
Choosing your mix

A practical mix for many women is this: receive income digitally so there is a record, keep most of the week's money in the account, and withdraw a set amount of cash once or twice a week for markets and transport. Pay bills and bigger purchases by transfer where the seller accepts it. Cash for the week then works like an envelope: when it is finished, you know you have reached your limit.
At the POS stand

Agree the charge first, watch the amount typed on the machine, take the printed or SMS receipt, and count the cash in front of the agent before you walk away. If the machine says 'declined' but you get a debit alert, do not repeat the withdrawal elsewhere until you have checked your balance and kept the reference.

Write yes or no beside each. Most people answer no to at least two. That is normal and it is the reason for this course. Be especially honest about the first question. People usually remember the big items, such as rent or a bag of rice, and forget the many small ones: the sachet water, the extra okada ride, the ₦200 airtime top-up done three times in a day. Those small, frequent costs are where most unplanned money goes.

If you share a household purse with a spouse or relatives, answer for the money that passes through your own hands, and note which costs someone else normally covers. That way your numbers stay true even when the household is complicated.
How many days could you cover?

One simple number shows how strong your position is: **days covered**. Add the money you have set aside (not money already promised to a bill), then divide it by what an average day costs your household. The answer is how many days you could keep going if income stopped.
Worked example: calculating days covered

For example, Funmi sells pap and akara in the mornings in Ibadan and also has a husband who contributes to the house. She wants to know how many days of household costs she could cover from her separate savings box.
She checks her savings box: ₦9,000. Her wallet app has ₦4,500 not yet promised to anything. Total reserve: ₦13,500.
From memory and a few receipts, household spending last week was about ₦21,000.
Days covered: ₦13,500 ÷ ₦3,000 = 4.5 days.
Funmi's reserve covers about four and a half days. Her starting goal is to reach seven days (₦21,000) by the end of the course, which means adding about ₦7,500 over four weeks, roughly ₦1,900 a week.
Use estimates now, real numbers later
Your 'average day' will be a rough guess at first. In Module 2 you will track real spending, then recalculate days covered with honest figures.
Securing your money accounts

Daily money now lives on your phone, so phone safety is money safety. Thieves rarely break into bank systems. They trick the owner, or they take a phone that has no lock. These steps take about fifteen minutes and protect everything you will build in this course.
Set a screen lock on your phone (PIN, pattern or fingerprint) that is not your birth year.
Turn on the lock inside each bank and wallet app.
Change any transaction PIN that is easy to guess, such as 1234, 0000 or your birthday.
Turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp so nobody can register your number on another phone without your code.
Write the official customer care number of each bank in a notebook kept at home, so you can block your account fast if your phone is stolen.
Learn your bank's short code for blocking an account, from the bank's website or a branch.
Never share these

Your card PIN, app password, OTP codes and BVN-linked security answers must never be given to anyone by phone, SMS or WhatsApp, even someone claiming to be from your bank, CBN, EFCC or a 'BVN update' office. Genuine institutions do not ask for them. If anyone asks, end the call.

This module turns the plan into a habit you can keep. You will set up a five-minute daily tracking routine on your phone or in a notebook, work through two weeks of real-looking records to find where money leaks, and learn a weekly review that corrects course before a small slip becomes a shortage.

Whatever you choose, use the same five columns: **date, what you bought, category, amount, and how you paid** (cash, transfer, card, wallet). The 'how you paid' column helps you match your record against your bank statement later.
Keep categories few

Too many categories make tracking slow. If you sell goods, try to keep stock money and household money apart, for example a separate wallet account for business. If they are mixed, at least label each entry Home or Business so you can see what the house really costs.

Repeating this short cycle every evening keeps your record honest and your next day planned.
During the day, note any spending above ₦100 as it happens: two words and an amount are enough ('bread 1,200').
In the evening, open your bank and wallet apps and scroll through today's transactions. Add anything you forgot.

Count the cash in your purse. Starting cash minus cash spent should equal what is left. If not, the difference is a forgotten purchase or money given away; record it as 'unknown' so the gap stays visible.

Worked example: closing one day
For example, Aisha is a hairdresser in Kano. She starts Tuesday with ₦6,000 cash and receives two transfers from customers. She uses a phone note for tracking.
Her note during the day reads: keke 400, gala and drink 700, relaxer stock 3,500 (business), kids' lunch 1,000.
In the evening she checks her wallet app and finds a ₦1,500 data purchase she had forgotten.
Cash check: she started with ₦6,000. Cash spends recorded: 400 + 700 + 3,500 + 1,000 = ₦5,600. Expected cash left: ₦400.
Her purse has ₦200. The ₦200 difference is recorded as 'unknown'.
Categories: Transport ₦400, Personal ₦700, Business ₦3,500, Children ₦1,000, Phone and data ₦1,500, Unknown ₦200.
Total spending for the day was ₦7,300, of which ₦3,800 was household spending. Without the evening check, she would have recorded only ₦5,600 and missed ₦1,700, about a quarter of the day.
Using Google Sheets if you prefer

If you are comfortable with Google Sheets, put your entries in rows with the amount in column D. In an empty cell type =SUM(D2:D50) to total the amounts. To total one category, type =SUMIF(C2:C50,"Transport",D2:D50), which adds every amount whose category in column C is Transport. The sheet updates itself as you add rows, and it works on the free Sheets phone app.
What to do when you miss a day

You will miss days. A child is ill, there is a long market day, or you simply forget. Do not abandon the record. The next morning, open your bank and wallet apps and copy yesterday's digital spending, then count your cash and write the difference from your last count as one line called 'cash, not itemised'. The total for the day is still correct even if the details are missing. Missing one day costs you a little detail; stopping the record for a week costs you the whole picture.

It also helps to attach the routine to something you already do every evening, such as charging your phone, saying night prayers or checking the children's homework. A habit tied to an existing habit is far easier to keep than one that needs a new reminder.
Data cost
Tracking needs almost no data. A notes app works offline, and Google Sheets can be set to work offline too. You do not need to buy extra data for this routine.

After two weeks of honest tracking you have something valuable: real numbers about your life. Now you turn them into decisions. This lesson shows how to total, compare and spot a **leak**, which means money that goes out in small amounts you did not really choose.
Step one: total by category
Add up each category for the two weeks. Then divide each category by the total and multiply by 100 to get its percentage. Percentages help because they let you compare weeks with different income.
Worked example: Blessing's two-week totals
For example, Blessing trades in children's clothes in Aba and tracked her household spending for 14 days. Her totals are illustrative.
Food and household ₦31,000; Transport ₦9,800; Phone and data ₦6,300; Bills ₦8,000; Children and school ₦7,500; Family and giving ₦6,000; Personal and wants ₦9,400. Total: ₦78,000.
Food share: ₦31,000 ÷ ₦78,000 × 100 ≈ 40%. Transport ≈ 13%. Personal and wants ≈ 12%. Phone and data ≈ 8%.
Looking inside Personal and wants, she finds 19 small items under ₦800: snacks, drinks, small gifts at the market. Together they come to ₦7,600.
Looking inside Phone and data, she finds she bought daily data bundles 9 times at ₦700 each: ₦6,300.
She compares this with a monthly plan from her network that gives enough data for her needs at a lower total cost per month (she checks the current price in her network's app).

Blessing finds two leaks: ₦7,600 in small unplanned buys and daily data bundles that cost more than a monthly plan would. She decides to fix the data first because it is a single decision, then put a ₦2,000-a-week cap on snacks.
Step two: look for the small, frequent items

Large costs are usually visible and planned. Leaks hide in items that are **small each time but frequent**. Use the grid below. Put each type of spending in a box by asking two questions: how often does this happen, and how much is it each time?

Step three: choose one leak and estimate the saving
Fix one leak at a time. Choose the one that is easiest to change and has the biggest weekly amount. Write the change as a rule you can follow, then estimate the saving with your own numbers.
Worked example: estimating a saving honestly
For example, Blessing sets a weekly snack cap of ₦2,000. Her snack spending averaged ₦7,600 over two weeks, which is ₦3,800 a week.
Weekly saving if she keeps the cap: ₦3,800 − ₦2,000 = ₦1,800.
Over four weeks: 4 × ₦1,800 = ₦7,200.
She plans for real life and assumes she keeps the rule three weeks out of four: 3 × ₦1,800 = ₦5,400.
A realistic estimate is about ₦5,400 a month, not the perfect ₦7,200. Honest estimates are easier to meet and keep motivation strong.
Cheaper ways to meet the same need
Not every fix is about spending less on a need. Often you can meet the same need for less money. Some examples that come up often in Nigerian households:

Data: compare the cost per gigabyte of daily, weekly and monthly bundles in your network's app or USSD menu. Longer bundles are often cheaper per gigabyte, but only if you actually use the data before it expires.
Transport: group errands into one trip, or share a ride with a neighbour going to the same market.

Food staples: buying rice, garri, beans or oil in a larger measure, alone or by sharing a bag with a friend, often costs less per cup than buying small daily quantities. Check the price per unit before deciding.
Cooking gas: refilling before the cylinder is completely empty avoids emergency trips and paying for a costlier alternative such as kerosene or ready food on the day it runs out.

Write the cost before and after for any change you make. A change only counts as a saving when your record shows it. Some changes save less than you hope, and that is useful to know too: it tells you to put your effort elsewhere.
Do not cut what keeps you well
A leak is spending that does not serve you. Food for your children, transport to work or market, and health care are not leaks, even when they are large. Cut wants and waste first.

Bills, Family Requests and Measuring Progress

Daily money is tested by the costs that come back every few weeks, by requests from family and friends, and by scams that target phone money. This module shows how to spread predictable bills across your weeks, how to handle money requests kindly and safely, and how to measure progress with a few honest numbers.
Predictable bills and a small buffer: no more 'surprise' costs

Start a small buffer for genuine surprises

Many money crises are not surprises at all. School fees come every term. The electricity token runs out every few weeks. The gas cylinder empties. Rent is due on the same date each year. These costs feel sudden because they do not come every week, so they are not in the weekly plan. This lesson brings them into the plan.
Make a list of returning costs

Look back over the last year, through your bank statement, your phone's payment history, receipts, and memory. Write every cost that returns but not weekly. For each, note roughly how much and how often. Use the prices you actually paid; prices change, so update the list each term.

Turn big costs into weekly amounts

Divide each cost by the number of weeks until it is due. That weekly figure becomes a line in your plan, moved to a separate place (a savings pocket in your bank or wallet app, or a labelled envelope) as soon as money comes in.
Worked example: spreading school fees and gas

For example, Chioma, a market trader in Onitsha, pays about ₦45,000 school fees per term for two children and refills a 12.5 kg gas cylinder roughly every six weeks for about ₦15,000. Prices are illustrative; use your own.
School fees: the next payment is due in 12 weeks. ₦45,000 ÷ 12 = ₦3,750 a week.
Gas: ₦15,000 every 6 weeks. ₦15,000 ÷ 6 = ₦2,500 a week.
Total to set aside each week: ₦3,750 + ₦2,500 = ₦6,250.
She opens two savings pockets in her bank app named 'Fees' and 'Gas' and moves the amounts every Saturday after market.
In week 6 she withdraws ₦15,000 for gas. In week 12 the Fees pocket holds 12 × ₦3,750 = ₦45,000.
Chioma pays both costs on time without borrowing. The weekly set-aside of ₦6,250 is far easier to find than ₦45,000 at once.
Start late? Catch up gradually

If the fee is due in 4 weeks and you have nothing saved, ₦45,000 ÷ 4 = ₦11,250 a week may be too much. Talk to the school early about paying in instalments, and set aside what you can. Asking early is better than missing the deadline.
Pay in the right order

When money is tight, the order you pay in matters. Pay what keeps the household safe and earning first, then fixed bills, then set-aside amounts, then wants. This protects you from paying for a want and then borrowing for food.

A small buffer for real surprises

Some costs truly are surprises: a phone screen breaks, a child needs clinic care, a roof leaks. A **buffer** is a small amount kept separately just for these. It is not for planned bills (those have their own pockets) and not for wants. Even ₦500 a week builds ₦26,000 in a year (52 × ₦500). The WODDI Savings, Spending and Budgeting course goes further on growing a full emergency fund; here the aim is simply to start.
Keep the buffer where it is easy to reach in an emergency but not mixed with daily money.
Decide in advance what counts as an emergency: health, safety, loss of income, urgent repairs.
When you use it, record why and plan how to rebuild it at your next weekly review.
Electricity tokens: plan by usage, not by panic

Prepaid electricity is a good example of a cost that feels random but is not. Look at your last three token purchases in your payment app or on the receipts. Note the amount and the date of each. If you bought ₦10,000 on the 2nd, the 23rd and the 14th of the next month, your household uses roughly ₦10,000 every three weeks, which is about ₦3,300 a week. Put that amount in a 'Light' pocket each week and buy the next token when the meter shows a few days of units left, not when the house is already dark. Buying through your bank or a trusted app also keeps the token number in your history if the SMS gets lost.
High-return offers are not a buffer

Never put bill or buffer money into a scheme that promises fast, high returns or pays you for bringing new members. Money you need on a set date must stay somewhere safe and boring, such as a licensed bank or wallet savings pocket.

Family requests, social obligations and money scams

Supporting family and community is part of life for most of us. Contributions for burials, weddings and naming ceremonies, school fees for a younger sibling, help for a parent in the village. These are good things. They become a problem only when they arrive with no plan, so that each request pulls money from food, bills or business stock.
Plan your giving

Add a **Family and giving** line to every weekly plan, sized to what you can truly afford. When a request comes, look at that line first. If there is money in it, you can give with a clear heart. If it is empty, you already know your answer, and you can offer something other than money or a smaller amount.
Worked example: answering three requests in one week
For example, Zainab is a civil servant in Abuja. Her weekly giving line is ₦5,000. This week she receives three requests.
Monday: her mother asks for ₦3,000 for drugs prescribed at the clinic. Zainab sends ₦3,000. Giving line left: ₦2,000.

Wednesday: a friend asks for ₦10,000 'until month end'. Zainab knows from past experience that such loans are often not repaid. She offers ₦2,000 as a gift she does not expect back, and says she cannot lend more this month.

Friday: a cousin's wedding committee asks every family member for ₦5,000. Her giving line is empty, so she replies that she will contribute ₦5,000 from next week's line, and she plans for it on Sunday.
Zainab supported all three people and kept her food, transport and bills money untouched. She spent exactly her ₦5,000 line this week and moved the wedding contribution into next week's plan.
Saying no, or not yet, kindly
Be honest and short: 'I can't send money this week, my money for this month is already committed.'
Offer what you can: a smaller amount, a later date you will keep, or practical help such as transport or food.
If you lend, decide in advance that you can afford to lose it, write the amount and the agreed return date, and keep the record.
Do not borrow to give. Borrowing to help someone else turns their problem into two problems.
Talking about giving at home

If you share household money with a spouse, agree the giving line together, including how requests from each side of the family will be handled. Many couples find it easier to agree a monthly amount for each family and stick to it than to debate every request as it arrives. Writing the agreement down, even in a WhatsApp message to each other, prevents later arguments about who gave what. When a large request comes, such as a parent's hospital bill, you can then decide together whether to use the buffer, contribute over several weeks, or share the cost with siblings.
When a request is a scam

Fraudsters take advantage of our kindness. A common trick is to take over someone's WhatsApp or create a new number with their profile photo, then message their contacts: 'I'm stranded, please send ₦20,000 to this account, I'll refund tomorrow.' The account name often does not match the person. Another trick is a **SIM swap**: a criminal gets your phone number moved to a new SIM, then receives your OTP codes and empties your accounts.

A two-minute check by voice call stops most impersonation scams.
Pause. Urgency is the scammer's main tool; a real relative can wait five minutes.
Call the person on the number you already had saved, not the one that messaged you. Ask a question only they would know.
Compare the account name with the person's real name. A mismatch is a strong warning sign.
Never send OTP codes, card details or your PIN to anyone, even a 'relative'.
If you were tricked, call your bank's official line at once to report it and request that the recipient account be flagged, and keep screenshots.
Signs of a SIM swap

If your phone suddenly shows 'No service' or 'Emergency calls only' in a place where it normally works, and you did not change anything, treat it as urgent. Use another phone to call your network provider and your bank, and ask the bank to block transactions until you confirm your SIM.
Fake 'send back my money' messages

Someone may send a fake credit SMS and then call, saying they sent money to you by mistake and asking you to refund it. Check your balance in your own app. If no money has truly arrived, send nothing. If money did arrive by mistake, ask the person to go through their bank to reverse it.

For example, Ruth runs a small fashion-design business in Jos and set herself the goal of stopping borrowing for food. Her average daily household cost is about ₦3,500. Figures are illustrative.

Read the trend, not one week

Any single week can be spoiled by a ceremony, an illness or a slow market. Look at the direction over three or four weeks. If the leak is falling and the buffer is rising, you are on track even if one week went over. If a number has not moved for three weeks, your fix is not working; change the rule rather than blaming yourself.
Calculating your real average daily cost

In Module 1 you guessed your daily cost. Now use your records. Add the household spending from your tracked weeks, leaving out business stock and money moved into bill pockets or the buffer, because those are not daily living costs. Divide by the number of days tracked. For example, if two weeks of household spending came to ₦49,000, the average day is ₦49,000 ÷ 14 = ₦3,500. Use this figure for days covered from now on, and recalculate it once a month as prices change.

Counting 'times borrowed' also needs a clear rule. Count every time you took money or goods on credit to meet a household need: a loan from a friend, food taken on credit from a shop, or a wallet app loan. Do not count business credit you planned, such as stock from a supplier with agreed payment terms. Writing the rule at the top of your table keeps the count honest from week to week.
Using the numbers to decide what to do next
Spending above plan for three weeks in a row: either the plan is unrealistic or a habit needs a new rule. Look at which category is causing it.
Leak not falling: the rule is too vague. Make it more specific, for example 'no snacks bought at the bus park' instead of 'fewer snacks'.
Set-aside balance falling: check whether it is being used for planned bills (fine) or for wants (needs a fix).
Still borrowing: look at the day of the week you borrow. It usually points to a gap day you can plan for.
Keep the same method every week
Use the same categories and the same way of counting each week. If you change how you calculate a number halfway, the trend is no longer a fair comparison.

Money habits rarely change in one person alone. If your husband buys the foodstuff, your children ask for pocket money, or your sister shares your house, their choices affect your record too. And the women in your community, church, mosque or WODDI circle face the same daily pressures. Sharing what works can help everyone, if it is done well.
Specific beats preachy

People switch off when they feel judged. 'You people waste money' starts an argument. 'I tracked my spending for two weeks and found I was spending about ₦2,000 a week on extra rides. Planning one trip on Saturday fixed most of it' starts a conversation. The second version is about you, uses a real number, and shows a simple change anyone could try.

Sharing your own experience with numbers invites others in instead of pushing them away.
A money talk at home
Choose a calm moment, not the day a bill is overdue. Keep it short, about fifteen minutes, and come with one page: your weekly plan or your progress table. Ask for one thing, not ten.
Start with what is going well: 'Our buffer has grown to ₦6,000 this month.'
Show one number that needs help: 'Light tokens cost us about ₦3,300 a week.'
Ask for ideas before giving yours: 'What could we do about it?'
Agree one action and who does it: 'We switch off the freezer at night when it is nearly empty; I will check the meter on Fridays.'
Agree when you will look at the number again.
Worked example: involving a teenager
For example, Patience, a petty trader in Benin City, gives her 15-year-old son ₦1,000 a day for transport and lunch, which is ₦5,000 for a five-day school week. He often asks for more by Thursday.
She shows him the weekly amount: 5 × ₦1,000 = ₦5,000, and explains that it is the household's plan, not a punishment.
She agrees to give him the full ₦5,000 on Monday instead of daily, with a simple record in his phone notes.
They agree that if he keeps a record and does not ask for more, any money left on Friday is his to keep.
After two weeks he has kept ₦600 and ₦900, and stopped asking for extra money midweek.
Patience's spending on her son stayed at ₦5,000 a week, the midweek requests stopped, and he started learning the same tracking habit she uses.
Sharing in a group

If you lead or attend a women's group, you can teach one method in ten minutes. The leak grid from Module 2 works well: draw the four boxes on a sheet of paper, ask each woman to name one small, frequent spend, and place it in the grid together. Do not ask anyone to say their income or debts aloud. Invite people to try one rule for a week and report back if they wish.
When the other person does not agree

Sometimes a spouse or relative is not interested, or feels that tracking means you do not trust them. Do not force it. Keep tracking the money that passes through your own hands, and let your results speak. A buffer that covers an unexpected clinic bill, or a month without borrowing, often persuades more than any argument. You can also start with a shared goal rather than a shared record: 'Let us have next term's school fees ready two weeks early.' People are more willing to work on a goal they care about than on a method they did not choose.

If money conversations at home regularly lead to anger, threats or one person taking control of the other's income, that is no longer a budgeting matter. Speak to someone you trust, a religious leader, a family elder or a support service, and keep your own important documents and a little money in a safe place.

Never share another person's figures, debts or money problems without their permission, including in WhatsApp groups. Do not pressure anyone to join a savings scheme, buy a product or lend money as part of a money talk. Your role is to share what worked for you, not to decide for others.

Choosing your next goal

Before you submit, open each file once more and check three things: the totals add up, the dates cover at least 14 days, and no account number, card number or BVN is visible. Ask a trusted person to look at your pattern report and tell you in one sentence what you changed and what it saved. If they can, your report is clear enough.

Your next goal should grow from your records, not from what someone else is doing. Look at your progress table. Which measure is weakest? That is usually the right place to focus. Make the goal specific, measurable and possible within 90 days, which is about 13 weeks.

Worked example: a 90-day buffer plan

For example, Amina sells fabrics in Sokoto. Her real average daily household cost is ₦4,000 and her buffer is ₦8,000, so she covers 2 days. Her goal is 14 days covered in 90 days. Figures are illustrative.
Amount still needed: ₦56,000 − ₦8,000 = ₦48,000.
Over 13 weeks: ₦48,000 ÷ 13 ≈ ₦3,700 a week.
Where it comes from: ₦2,200 a week from the transport leak she already fixed, and ₦1,500 a week from reducing wants.
Checkpoints: about ₦23,000 in the buffer by week 4 (₦8,000 + 4 × ₦3,700 = ₦22,800), about ₦38,000 by week 8, and ₦56,000 by week 13.
Amina's plan turns a big goal into ₦3,700 a week, funded from changes she has already proved she can make, with three checkpoints to tell her if she is on track.

Checkpoints every four weeks show early if the plan needs adjusting.
Keeping the habits going
Keep the five-minute daily routine, but you may reduce detail: category and amount only.
Keep the weekly review on the same day, and add a line for progress toward your 90-day goal.
Move set-aside amounts on the day money arrives, before spending starts.
Recalculate your average daily cost and update bill amounts once a month, because prices change.
At each checkpoint, if you are behind, reduce the target or find one more leak; do not abandon the plan.
Planning for the hard weeks ahead

Ninety days will include at least one difficult week: a festival season, a slow market, a price rise or a family event. Look at your calendar now and mark the weeks you already know will be expensive, such as the start of a school term, Christmas, Sallah or a planned family ceremony. For those weeks, either lower the set-aside amount on purpose or save a little extra in the weeks before. A plan that expects hard weeks survives them. A plan that assumes every week is normal tends to collapse at the first surprise.

Also decide now what you will do if income drops for several weeks. Write a short 'lean week' version of your plan: the needs only, with wants and most set-aside amounts paused, and the buffer used for food and essentials if necessary. Having it written means you can switch to it calmly instead of borrowing in a panic.
Make it automatic where you can

Many bank and wallet apps let you set up a recurring transfer into a savings pocket on a fixed day. If yours does, set it for the day after your income usually arrives. Money that moves automatically is money you do not have to decide about each week.

Why this matters
Money in: salary, sales, transfers
Money waiting: purse, bank, wallet app
Money out: food, transport, bills, gifts
The plan gives each naira a job
Two women can earn about the same and live very differently. Often the difference is not income. It is how daily money decisions are made.
Every household has three parts. Money in is everything you receive: salary, sales, payment for a service, or money from family.
Money waiting is where it sits before you use it: your purse, a box at home, a bank account, or a wallet app.
Money out is everything you spend or give: food, transport, data, school costs, rent and contributions.
The step most people skip is the plan. Without it, money is spent in the order requests appear, and the loudest need wins.
Worked example
Finding the gap days in a salary month
For example, Ngozi, a school administrator in Enugu, is paid about 120,000 naira a month.
Week 1 spending
Week 2, with unplanned shoes
Week 3 spending
Illustrative figures from the course.
Here is a worked example. Ngozi is paid about 120,000 naira at the end of each month. She keeps no plan and spends as needs appear.
In week 1 she spends 48,000 naira. In week 2 she spends 36,000, including shoes for 12,000 that were not planned. In week 3 she spends 28,000.
That is 112,000 naira gone in three weeks, leaving only 8,000. Week 4 still needs transport and food, so she is about 10,000 short and borrows.
The problem was not low pay. It was front-loading. With a plan, she releases 30,000 naira each week, and the week four gap disappears.
Step by step
Give each naira a job
Plan in weeks, even if you are paid monthly.
Write the money you expect, and the day
List fixed jobs: food, transport, bills, stock
Set something aside, even 500 naira
Add wants last, with a clear limit
Too high? Cut wants first
On one notebook page or in your notes app, write the money you expect this week, and the day it arrives.
Then list the fixed jobs first: food, transport to work or market, bills due, and business stock.
Add an amount to set aside, even 500 naira.
If the total is too high, reduce wants first, before spending starts, not after you run out.
And plan in weeks. Seven days is short enough to remember and long enough to see a pattern.
Use each for what it does well
Cash is accepted almost everywhere and needs no network. But it leaves no record, and it is easy to lose or overspend.
Digital money leaves a record and is safer for large sums. But small charges add up, and you must protect your PIN.
Always look before you confirm. Read the fee line on the app screen, and ask the POS agent the charge out loud before the card goes in.
What small charges cost in a month
For example, Halima runs a provisions kiosk in Kaduna and withdraws from a POS agent almost daily.
Old way: 5 withdrawals x 200
Old way, monthly
New way: 2 withdrawals x 400
New way, monthly
Charges are illustrative. Use your agent's real figures.
Halima withdraws 10,000 naira five days a week, and her agent charges about 200 naira each time.
That is 1,000 naira a week, or about 4,000 naira a month, just in charges.
She changes her routine. She pays her main supplier by transfer and withdraws 25,000 twice a week. The agent charges about 400 each time, so about 3,200 a month.
She saves about 800 naira a month, makes fewer cash trips, and now has a record of supplier payments. A small change in habit made the difference.
Safety first
Lock down your money accounts
Never share your PIN, password or OTP with anyone.
Screen lock that is not your birth year
Turn on the lock inside each money app
Change easy PINs like 1234 or 0000
WhatsApp two-step verification on

Phone safety is money safety. Thieves rarely break into banks. They trick the owner, or take a phone with no lock.
Set a screen lock that is not your birth year, and turn on the lock inside each bank and wallet app.
Change any PIN that is easy to guess, like 1234, 0000 or your birthday. Turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp.
Write your bank's official customer care number in a notebook at home, so you can block your account fast if your phone is stolen.
No genuine bank, agent or office will ask for your PIN, password or OTP. If anyone asks, end the call. And never trust an SMS alert alone. Check your balance in your own app.

Why this matters

Many money crises are not surprises at all. School fees come every term. The electricity token and the gas cylinder run out every few weeks.
Rent is due on the same date each year, and ceremonies come several times a year.
They feel sudden only because they are not in the weekly plan. This module brings them in.
Worked example
Spreading school fees and gas
For example, Chioma, a market trader in Onitsha, has school fees and a gas refill to plan for.
Fees: 45,000 over 12 weeks
Gas: 15,000 every 6 weeks
Illustrative prices. Use your own.
Here is the method. Divide each big cost by the number of weeks until it is due. That weekly figure becomes a line in your plan.
Chioma pays about 45,000 naira school fees per term for two children, and refills her 12.5 kilogram gas cylinder about every six weeks for about 15,000.
The fees are due in 12 weeks. 45,000 divided by 12 is 3,750 naira a week.
Gas is 15,000 divided by 6, which is 2,500 a week.
Together that is 6,250 naira a week. She moves it every Saturday into two savings pockets in her bank app, named Fees and Gas.
In week 12 the Fees pocket holds the full 45,000, and she pays without borrowing.
When money is tight
Pay from the base up
Bill set-aside amounts
A small buffer
Wants and extras last
When money is tight, the order matters. Pay for food, water and health first. Then rent, light and transport to work.

Then your bill set-aside amounts, then a small buffer. A buffer is money kept separately only for real surprises, like a broken phone screen or a clinic visit. Even 500 naira a week builds 26,000 in a year.
Wants come last, and they are the first to cut. This stops you paying for a want and then borrowing for food.
Family and giving
Answering three requests in one week
For example, Zainab, a civil servant in Abuja, keeps a weekly giving line of 5,000 naira.
Monday: mother's drugs
Wednesday: gift to a friend
Friday: wedding, from next week
Giving comes from the giving line only.
Supporting family is a good thing. It becomes a problem only when each request pulls money from food, bills or stock. So add a family and giving line to every weekly plan.
On Monday, Zainab's mother asks for 3,000 naira for drugs from the clinic. She sends it. 2,000 is left.
On Wednesday, a friend asks to borrow 10,000 until month end. Zainab offers 2,000 as a gift she does not expect back, and says kindly she cannot lend more this month.
On Friday, a wedding committee asks for 5,000. Her line is empty, so she promises it from next week's line.
She helped all three people and kept her food and bills money untouched. And remember: do not borrow to give.

Never send OTP codes, card details or your PIN to anyone.

Check the account name matches
Tricked? Call your bank's official line
Fraudsters take over someone's WhatsApp, or copy their profile photo, then message: I'm stranded, please send 20,000 naira.
Pause. Urgency is the scammer's main tool. A real relative can wait five minutes.
Call the person on the number you already had saved, not the one that messaged you. Compare the account name with their real name. A mismatch is a strong warning sign.
Never send OTP codes, card details or your PIN. If you were tricked, call your bank's official line at once and keep screenshots.
And if your phone suddenly shows no service where it normally works, it could be a SIM swap. Use another phone to call your network and your bank straight away.
Every week
Five honest numbers
Feelings change with mood. Numbers show real progress. Each week, write five: spending versus plan, your leak amount, your buffer and bill pockets, days covered, and how many times you borrowed.

Ruth in Jos saw her leak fall from 3,900 to 1,800 naira a week, and her buffer grow from 2,000 to 6,000, over four weeks. Week 3 looked bad on its own because of a burial, but the trend was steady improvement.
So read the trend over three or four weeks, not one week, and keep the same method every time.
Key points
Remember
Weekly set-aside = cost divided by weeks left
Pay food and safety first, wants last
Give from a planned giving line
Call a trusted number before you send
Judge progress by the trend

To remember. Divide each big bill by the weeks until it is due. Pay food and safety first, wants last. Give from a planned giving line. Call a number you trust before sending money. And judge your progress by the trend, not one week.

Talking about money
Money habits rarely change in one person alone. But people switch off when they feel judged. Saying 'you people waste money' starts an argument.
Instead, share your own result with a real number. For example: I found I was spending about 2,000 naira a week on extra rides, and planning one trip on Saturday fixed most of it.
